cf.title: Fix interval input at minimum signed field values

input.subject: [PATCH] Fix interval input at minimum signed field values (BUG #19746)

verdict_reasoning: The goal is a reported bug fix (BUG #19746) and nothing at levels 1a or 1b is in question. The one surviving objection, standards-compat-1, is fixable: message #2 lists four inputs that master accepts and v2 rejects when the minimum field comes last. A fix that may go to back branches must not reject input accepted before, so a revised version is needed before commit.

brief.title: Fix interval input rejecting minimum signed field values
brief.problem: Interval output can contain INT64_MIN microseconds, or minimum day and month values in postgres_verbose style with AGO, but interval input rejects that text. So a value that prints cannot be read back, and the bug report's pg_dump example restores no rows. Anyone who dumps and restores or round-trips such intervals as text is affected.
brief.proposed_design: DecodeInterval in datetime.c applies the effective sign of time fields before checked accumulation, so INT64_MIN microseconds parse. It applies AGO while accumulating numeric fields instead of negating at the end, to handle the minimum day and month in verbose output. The commit message says cancellation between fields near the limits stays possible and out-of-range totals are rejected.
user_visible_surface: Interval text input accepts values at the minimum signed microsecond, day and month boundaries that it rejected before.
Some inputs that were already invalid now get a different error, such as "invalid input syntax" instead of "field value out of range" for a repeated unit.
author_claims: The bug lets an interval with INT64_MIN microseconds print but fail when read back.
The patch keeps cancellation between fields near the limits.
New regression tests cover text round trips, boundary values, overflow and AGO output.
brief.thread_state: Ishjaap Singh tested v2 and confirmed the reported cases and the pg_dump example are fixed, but found four inputs that work on master and fail with v2 when the minimum field comes last in the string. He asked for tests of both field orders, and no v3 is visible.
unclear: The material does not show whether the author will fix the field-order regression that the reviewer found.
The material does not say which branches get the fix; v2 does not apply to REL_15 and REL_16.
The material does not say whether the changed error message for invalid input is intended.

objections.title: v2 breaks interval inputs that master accepts when the minimum field comes last
objections.failure_scenario: An application or a stored view default uses an interval literal such as '1 week -2147483648 days ago'. Master accepts it. After a minor release with v2 it fails with "interval field value out of range". The user finds out when a query, a restore or a CHECK constraint errors after upgrade.
objections.argument: Message #2 shows four inputs that work on unpatched master and fail with v2. In each, DecodeInterval negates the minimum field first because it reads right to left. A bugfix meant for back branches must not reject input that minor releases accepted before, because back-branch users do not expect behaviour changes. The commit message promises that cancellation is preserved, but v2 keeps it for only one field order, and no v3 is visible.
objections.author_must_show: Does a revised version accept all four inputs from message #2, with regression tests for both field orders?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 lists four inputs that return true on unpatched master and fail with v2, and no v3 or author reply is visible. The commit message claims cancellation is preserved, so the material confirms the regression and does not answer it.

refuted.title: Moving negation per field repeats the one-symptom fix pattern
refuted.failure_scenario: A user stores '1 week -2147483648 days ago' or a similar mixed-field interval. On master it reads back, but with v2 it fails with "interval field value out of range". A restore or an application upgrade on a minor release is where this shows up.
refuted.argument: [P2] was withdrawn because a fix to one output path left the same unsafe-negation assumption in other places. Message #2 shows v2 has the same shape. It applies the sign per field, right to left, so overflow now depends on field order and breaks inputs that work on master. The commit message claims cancellation is preserved, but the only tests put the minimum field first.
refuted.author_must_show: Does the new design accumulate signed fields so the result is independent of field order, with tests of every order from message #2?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which states the field-order regression without a precedent. [P2] concerned a fix to one EncodeInterval output path and must not be used as support here.

refuted.title: Branch scope of the round-trip fix is not stated
refuted.failure_scenario: A user on REL_16 dumps a table holding an INT64_MIN-microsecond interval. Fixed branches can restore it, but an unpatched 15 or 16 server still restores no rows. The user finds out only when the restored table comes up empty.
refuted.argument: Message #2 reports that v2 applies to master and REL_17-19 but not to REL_15/16, while REL_14 does not show the bug. The proposal does not say which branches get the fix or whether 15 and 16 need a separate version. A text-format pg_dump round trip that works on some supported branches and not on others gives users a data-loss case that depends on the minor version.
refuted.author_must_show: Which supported branches will get the fix, and will REL_15/16 get their own version so that every affected branch can restore its own dumps?

critic.reasoning: The scenario describes the existing bug on REL_15/16, which the patch does not cause or worsen. The committer usually decides the back-patch range and adapts the patch per branch at commit time, so this is not a design flaw.

refuted.title: Sign handling during accumulation makes overflow depend on field order
refuted.failure_scenario: A user stores '1 week -2147483648 days ago', which works on master. After a minor release with v2, the same text fails with "interval field value out of range". Dumps and application input that worked before stop loading, and users find out only when the restore or insert fails.
refuted.argument: DecodeInterval reads fields right to left. v2 applies the sign and AGO during checked accumulation, so the result now depends on which field comes first in the string (message #2). The commit message promises that cancellation near the limits still works, but the tests cover only one field order. A future change to field handling can break the other order again, and no test would catch it. A bug fix that adds a regression in a back branch is harder to defend than the bug it fixes.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the accumulation use a wider intermediate or check range only on the final total, so the result does not depend on field order, with tests for both orders?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The failure scenario and the evidence from message #2 are the same, and the maintenance point depends only on the missing tests for the second field order.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: The fix lets text dumps of minimum-value intervals restore, but v2 rejects some interval text that master accepts.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: It is a bug fix in DecodeInterval; v2 applies to master and REL_17-19 but not REL_15/16, and changes accepted input.

doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Will a revised version accept the four inputs from message #2 that work on master and fail with v2?
How does the revised accumulation make the result independent of the order of fields in the input string?
Will the regression tests cover cancellation near the limits with the minimum field both first and last in the string?
Which branches is the fix meant for, and is a separate version planned for REL_15 and REL_16?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the datetime and interval input code in datetime.c and the back-patch rules for input behaviour.
committability.liability: The owner signs for interval text input behaviour on every branch that gets the fix, including any input that was accepted before and is rejected after a minor release.
committability.author_follow_up: The author registered the CommitFest entry on 2026-11-10, after message #2 suggested it, but no reply or v3 is visible.

priority.reason: The patch is small and touches only datetime.c and the interval tests, and it fixes a reported dump and restore failure at boundary values. Message #2 found a field-order regression against master, so v2 needs a revision before further review.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the cause of the field-order regression rests on message #2. Whether other field combinations or input styles regress cannot be judged without the code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Show subtransaction overflow status
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch exposes each backend's subtransaction count and whether its subtransaction cache has overflowed, so DBAs can find the sessions that force SLRU lookups for all concurrent queries. It started as two new pg_stat_activity columns and was reworked into a single function returning a record per backend.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that effort should go into fixing the subtransaction overflow performance problem itself, because monitoring does not relieve the problem and could cause compatibility problems once a fundamental fix changes how this area works. Andres Freund agreed and asked for the entry to be marked rejected, also noting it had been failing on cfbot for weeks. The author agreed that a real fix would make the status reporting pointless and marked it rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If the subxact overflow business is causing
real-world performance problems, let's find a way to fix that, not put
effort into monitoring tools that do little to actually alleviate anyone's
pain.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix formatting of Interval output
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch special-cased INT_MIN hours in EncodeInterval, so that abs() no longer prints a value such as '--2147483648:00:00'. It fixed only that one output path.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane noted that three of the four formats in EncodeInterval assume -x or abs(x) is safe, and that interval2tm can overflow on values Postgres computed successfully, so fixing one symptom was not enough. He suggested int64 arithmetic in a new struct for intervals in place of struct pg_tm. The author withdrew the entry and moved the work to his related commitfest patch 3541.

precedents_retrieved.title: Nonreplayable XLog records by means of overflows and >MaxAllocSize lengths
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds checks in xloginsert.c so that the WAL insertion API cannot assemble a record larger than xlogreader can read (MaxAllocSize, later a fixed 1020 MiB limit), and cannot overflow xl_tot_len through repeated XLogRegisterData() calls. It also documents the record size limit in the XLogRecord spec.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier committed part of the patch, the API changes and the uint16 block data checks. He then asked for a rebase of the rest, and the author did not reply for two commitfests, so the entry was returned with feedback. After it was closed, Andres Freund noted that the new record-too-large ERROR usually happens inside a critical section and so becomes a PANIC. He suggested building large records such as the commit record before the critical section.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
No replies after 4 weeks, so I have marked this entry as returned
with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve overflow checks potentially optimized away by compiler
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal rewrites signed-integer overflow checks such as x + y < x into precondition tests such as x > INT_MAX - y, so compilers that treat signed overflow as undefined (icc, pathcc, clang) cannot remove them. Later versions extended this to int.c, int8.c and btree_gist, added INT16 overflow macros and added regression tests.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took up the final version, so Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback. Earlier, Greg Stark wrote that he was coming around to Tom's view that the change was a lot of hassle for little gain. Tom's own message giving that view is not among the visible messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: And nobody got interested into that, marking as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: abs function for interval
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an abs() function and an @ operator for the interval type. The goal is to compare the size of a timestamp difference without knowing which timestamp is larger.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund found that the patch checks the sign of each interval field separately, so abs('1 day -1 second') flips only the seconds. He also expected overflow failures for values such as '-2147483648 days' and found the tests too weak. The author agreed to rework the patch but sent no new version, and Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback after four weeks.

precedents_retrieved.title: Multiple passwords, interval expirations
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves role passwords into a new catalog, pg_auth_password, so a role can have several named passwords at once, each with its own expiration. A GUC (password_valid_duration) or new SQL grammar sets the expiration as an interval, so users can add a new password before the old one expires during rotation.

Design questions were still open in the last shown discussion: syntax for N passwords, whether passwords need names, and how a client gets the shared SCRAM salt to compute a secret with PQencryptPasswordConn().

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert ill-considered change in pg_resetwal output.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert ill-considered change in pg_resetwal output.
Reverted commit(s): Use the terminology "WAL file" not "log file" more consistently.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 31dcfae83 changed one pg_resetwal output string, and a
corresponding test in pg_upgrade, without sufficient thought for
the consequences.  We can't change that output without creating
hazards for cross-version upgrades, since pg_upgrade needs to be able
to read the output of several different versions of pg_resetwal.
There may well be external tools with the same requirement.

For the moment, just revert those two changes.  What we really
ought to do here is have a separate, stable, easily machine-readable
output format for pg_resetwal and pg_controldata, as proposed
years ago by Alvaro.  Once that's in place and tools no longer
need to depend on the exact spelling of the human-readable output,
we can put back this change.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert my bad decision of about a year ago to make PortalDefineQuery responsible for copying the query string into the new Portal.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert my bad decision of about a year ago to make PortalDefineQuery responsible for copying the query string into the new Portal.  Such copying is unnecessary in the common code path through exec_simple_query, and in this case it can be enormously expensive because the string might contain a large number of individual commands; we were copying the entire, long string for each command, resulting in O(N^2) behavior for N commands. (This is the cause of bug #4079.)  A second problem with it is that PortalDefineQuery really can't risk error, because if it elog's before having set up the Portal, we will leak the plancache refcount that the caller is trying to hand off to the portal.  So go back to the design in which the caller is responsible for making sure everything is copied into the portal if necessary.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert refactoring of hex code to src/common/
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert refactoring of hex code to src/common/
Reverted commit(s): move hex_decode() to /common so it can be called from frontend; Rework refactoring of hex and encoding routines; Remove PG_SHA*_DIGEST_STRING_LENGTH from sha2.h
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This is a combined revert of the following commits:
- c3826f8, a refactoring piece that moved the hex decoding code to
src/common/.  This code was cleaned up by aef8948, as it originally
included no overflow checks in the same way as the base64 routines in
src/common/ used by SCRAM, making it unsafe for its purpose.
- aef8948, a more advanced refactoring of the hex encoding/decoding code
to src/common/ that added sanity checks on the result buffer for hex
decoding and encoding.  As reported by Hans Buschmann, those overflow
checks are expensive, and it is possible to see a performance drop in
the decoding/encoding of bytea or LOs the longer they are.  Simple SQLs
working on large bytea values show a clear difference in perf profile.
- ccf4e27, a cleanup made possible by aef8948.

The reverts of all those commits bring back the performance of hex
decoding and encoding back to what it was in ~13.  Fow now and
post-beta3, this is the simplest option.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add missing function abs (interval)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a built-in abs(interval) function and @ operator, defined as the larger of x and -x, to match the other types that have unary minus. The author also proposed changing interval_smaller and interval_larger so that min(interval) and max(interval) return the first of several values that compare equal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding. Tom Lane objected that the GREATEST(x, -x) definition leaves the result for intervals equal to zero, such as '1 month -30 days', to an implementation detail, and that the min/max change only moves the odd results to other cases. He suggested a CASE WHEN x < '0'::interval formulation, and the author agreed to send a revised patch but never did, so the entry was returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Sequence Access Methods, round two
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds sequence access methods, with a USING clause for CREATE SEQUENCE, a callback interface modeled on table and index AMs, and a default_sequence_access_method GUC, so that nextval() and setval() can use custom computation such as cluster-wide or snowflake sequences. It moves the in-core sequence logic into a "seqlocal" AM, adds pg_dump support, and ships a snowflake contrib module.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last visible messages are rebases and small reviews from Kirill Reshke, Chao Li and others, with no deciding objection. Early on, Peter Eisentraut asked for the use cases to be explained and for a real implementation instead of a test module. The author later wrote that an unconference session reached no consensus and that few people were interested.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
Reverted commit(s): Further reduce overhead for passing plpgsql variables to the executor.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This patch does three interrelated things:

* Create a new expression execution step type EEOP_PARAM_CALLBACK
and add the infrastructure needed for add-on modules to generate that.
As discussed, the best control mechanism for that seems to be to add
another hook function to ParamListInfo, which will be called by
ExecInitExpr if it's supplied and a PARAM_EXTERN Param is found.
For stand-alone expressions, we add a new entry point to allow the
ParamListInfo to be specified directly, since it can't be retrieved
from the parent plan node's EState.

* Redesign the API for the ParamListInfo paramFetch hook so that the
ParamExternData array can be entirely virtual.  This also lets us get rid
of ParamListInfo.paramMask, instead leaving it to the paramFetch hook to
decide which param IDs should be accessible or not.  plpgsql_param_fetch
was already doing the identical masking check, so having callers do it too
seemed redundant.  While I was at it, I added a "speculative" flag to
paramFetch that the planner can specify as TRUE to avoid unwanted failures.
This solves an ancient problem for plpgsql that it couldn't provide values
of non-DTYPE_VAR variables to the planner for fear of triggering premature
"record not assigned yet" or "field not found" errors during planning.

* Rework plpgsql to get rid of the need for "unshared" parameter lists,
by dint of turning the single ParamListInfo per estate into a nearly
read-only data structure that doesn't instantiate any per-variable data.
Instead, the paramFetch hook controls access to per-variable data and can
make the right decisions on the fly, replacing the cases that we used to
need multiple ParamListInfos for.  This might perhaps have been a
performance loss on its own, but by using a paramCompile hook we can
bypass plpgsql_param_fetch entirely during normal query execution.
(It's now only called when, eg, we copy the ParamListInfo into a cursor
portal.  copyParamList() or SerializeParamList() effectively instantiate
the virtual parameter array as a simple physical array without a
paramFetch hook, which is what we want in those cases.)  This allows
reverting most of commit 6c82d8d1f, though I kept the cosmetic
code-consolidation aspects of that (eg the assign_simple_var function).

Performance testing shows this to be at worst a break-even change,
and it can provide wins ranging up to 20% in test cases involving
accesses to fields of "record" variables.  The fact that values of
such variables can now be exposed to the planner might produce wins
in some situations, too, but I've not pursued that angle.

In passing, remove the "parent" pointer from the arguments to
ExecInitExprRec and related functions, instead storing that pointer in a
transient field in ExprState.  The ParamListInfo pointer for a stand-alone
expression is handled the same way; we'd otherwise have had to add
yet another recursively-passed-down argument in expression compilation.

roaster_notes.note: One objection, fixable. [P5] concerns abs() for interval and was skipped because only keywords overlap.
The changed error message for repeated units was judged acceptable in message #2, so it is not raised here. No precedent's recorded reason applies to an input-side fix.

The patch changes only the text input path in DecodeInterval. The on-disk and binary interval format, WAL, catalogs, the wire protocol and the ABI stay the same. Dump and restore of boundary values gets better. The field-order regression in message #2 affects parsing semantics and belongs to other angles.

The proposal changes how interval text input parses minimum signed field values and has no privilege or exposure aspect. It adds no new privilege, function, view or setting, and it does not change who may call interval input. The changed error message reveals nothing about other users' data, and parsing a short string adds no unbounded memory, disk, lock or worker cost.
The fix stays inside datetime.c and adds no cost to hot paths. Making text output read back as input is a core invariant and belongs in core.

This is a bug fix for interval text input that rejects values interval output produces, and no existing feature, option or extension lets such a value be read back. Binary send/recv avoids the problem but does not help text dumps or the pg_dump example, so nothing from this angle applies.

No demand objection applies. The proposal fixes a reported bug (BUG #19746): interval output that cannot be read back, so a pg_dump example restores no rows (message #2). Dump and restore correctness needs no demand case, and the cost falls only on the interval input path. The field-order regression in message #2 is a design matter for other angles.
